item.title: U.S. offers $20 million for information on Iran's nuclear program
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: The U.S. military's Central Command announced Friday it is offering up to $20 million and possible relocation in exchange for information about Iran's nuclear program, its facilities, equipment or personnel.President Trump confirmed on Friday the U.S. carried out "minor strikes" on Iran, after local state media reported missiles striking Qeshm island in the Strait of HormuzAn Iranian army spokesman quoted by Iranian state media said Saturday the country was "stronger" than at the beginning of the war with the U.S. and Israel. The spokesman added the Iranian military gained experience from the "direct confrontation."
New Updates
3:26 AM
Trump confirms U.S. carried out more "minor strikes" on Iran
President Trump confirmed on Friday the U.S. carried out "minor strikes" in Iran, after local state media reported missiles striking Qeshm Island on the Strait of Hormuz.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Mr. Trump was asked whether the U.S. carried out more strikes on the island.
"I don't want to talk about it," the president said. "We do minor strikes. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe 5."
On Saturday, Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that two missiles had struck Qeshm island, added that there was no official information on the damage. Iranian state television also reported two explosions on the island.

item.title: Pope voted in U.S. election because he's "proud to be an American"
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV, who became the first sitting pontiff to vote in a U.S. election, said Friday he is "proud to be an American and to exercise my right" to vote.
His remarks, made to reporters en route to Latin America for a 12-day trip, come after the Vatican confirmed the U.S.-born pontiff had voted via mail-in ballot in his native Chicago. He declined to comment on the outcome of the midterm elections, which gave control of Congress to the Democrats in a repudiation of President Trump. Instead, he pointed to the statement released by the Vatican last week that cited his longstanding belief in civic participation.
The pope, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said in an Oct. 30 statement.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Vatican said in a statement.
Pope Leo XIV meets with the media on the papal flight from Rome to Montevideo, starting his Apostolic Journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6, 2026, in Rome, Italy.
Simone Risoluti - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool / Getty Images
The pope has a long history of civic engagement in the U.S., the Vatican said, confirming that during his nearly two decades as a missionary and then bishop in Peru, Leo voted whenever he was eligible. He holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.
The Associated Press reported Leo, as Robert Prevost, previously voted in five primary elections since 2000 — on the Democratic ballots in 2008 and 2019 and Republican ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.

item.title: Thomas Markle Sr., Meghan's father, arrested in Florida
item.description:
Thomas Markle Sr., the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was arrested Friday in Florida in connection with allegations he possessed child sex abuse material in storage units in California, the Justice Department announced.
The announcement came after three sources familiar with the matter confirmed the arrest to CBS News.
The Justice Department said Markle was arrested for allegedly keeping child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades.
"These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.
Markle, who made his first court appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday, entered the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing black pants and a black T-shirt with an illustration of a cat drinking a tropical drink.
Markle was advised that this hearing was related to the items found in two storage units in California. Prosecutors said they have not made a determination on whether he stays in Florida or is transferred to California, where the charges originated.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Thomas Wilson ordered Markle released on personal recognizance and ordered him to submit to home detention and electronic monitoring. Markle is also not permitted to travel outside the Middle District of Florida and the Central District of California.
No plea was taken. Markle's arraignment date in the Central District of California is not yet scheduled, but likely won't happen for at least several weeks.
The Daily Mail, a British tabloid newspaper, first reported Markle's arrest.

item.title: Ukrainian official sees hope for eventual Putin-Zelenskyy meeting
item.description:
KYIV, Ukraine — Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine's Presidential Office, expressed "restrained optimism" there could be progress made toward an eventual meeting between Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin during trilateral negotiations next week.
Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 for the first trilateral talks since February and the first since a heated back-and-forth over SpaceX's Starshield being throttled down. In an interview with CBS News on Friday, Budanov said the discussions would focus on postwar security guarantees for Ukraine and Russia.
"There are absolutely different situations at different times," Budanov said, referring to these trilateral discussions versus the ones in February. "Now, obviously, all parties wanted to hold this meeting. This means that there are certain prerequisites for this."
"These negotiations are not the last," he said.
Budanov, who led the country's Defense Intelligence service before taking over Ukraine's Presidential Office in January, will join the delegation led by Ukraine's top negotiator, Rustem Umerov. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to represent Washington. Russia's delegation will be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a Vladimir Putin aide who headed Moscow's team in earlier rounds of negotiations.
"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said in announcing the talks earlier this week.
Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine Kyrylo Budanov, left, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during talks with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Kyiv, Ukraine, Sept. 6, 2026.

item.title: Hoax bomb threats affect at least 20 European flights within hours
item.description:
Paris — At least 20 commercial flights in Europe had to deal with bomb threats Thursday, with at least one being diverted to a military base in France. While authorities have reported no explosives discovered on any of the jets, and they all appeared to be hoaxes, Thursday's incidents add to a fast-growing number of journeys hit by similar threats this week, which one expert said suggested a "very deliberate act."
British authorities dismissed threats to about seven flights earlier this week as hoaxes, but the number of impacted journeys soared to at least 27 on Thursday, meaning significant disruption for thousands of passengers and raising concerns about a possible coordinated effort to impact travel on the continent.
At least two more European flights, along with several Irish and British news outlets, got similar threats on Friday.
No authorities have confirmed a link between any of the threats, but Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Friday that Europe appeared to be facing "hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare."
David Kaminski-Morrow, Air Transport Editor with FlightGlobal, declined to speculate on who might be behind the threats to commercial flights this week, but he noted that "we currently live in a time of political aggression in regions including Europe, and it's a pretty effective tactic if someone is looking to cause disruption."
"The cluster of threats seems unusual, but it's hard to determine the extent to which they might be organized," he said, noting that "the publicity alone could spur further threats unrelated to earlier ones."
An Aer Lingus Airbus A320 plane is seen at Evreux military air base after the flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to France following a bomb threat, Nov. 5, 2026.
Gonzalo Fuentes/REUTERS

item.title: Doomsday cult leader learns fate for murders of 190 children
item.description:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult linked to the deaths of more than 400 people was sentenced on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people.
The High Court in Kenya's coastal city of Mombasa issued the sentence for Pastor Paul Mackenzie. He was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult after he ordered his followers to starve themselves to death in order to meet Jesus.
Justice Diana Kavedza said that Mackenzie, leader of the Good News International Church, bore the "primary criminal culpability" for relocating his followers to a remote location and ordering them to fast to death.
Mackenzie was charged with the murders alongside 28 of his followers, including guards who enforced his fasting directives and gravediggers who helped conceal the mass graves. All denied the charges, except for one person who confessed and pleaded for leniency.
On Oct. 19, the court found all 29 of the accused guilty of the murder of 191 people.
In 2023, more than 400 bodies were exhumed from shallow graves on the 800-acre Chakama Ranch in coastal Kilifi County, where Mackenzie's followers lived in mud huts, away from the scrutiny of local communities and authorities.
More than 60 bodies were positively identified and reburied by their relatives, while many others remain unidentified and unclaimed.
During the sentencing, Kavedza said that 183 victims died of starvation, defined as a complete lack of food, and the other eight were classified as murder by direct homicide.

item.title: 3 charged with using AI to steal some $129 million from companies
item.description:
New York — Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, prosecutors said Thursday.
Over more than a year and a half, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, targeted thousands of companies across the world in their AI scheme, according to the indictment filed in a U.S. District Court in New York.
Their victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the United Kingdom, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida, according to court documents.
The defendants, from Spain, the U.K., Israel and the United Arab Emirates, were also charged with money laundering, according to the indictment.
Lawyers for Soall and Sheetrit didn't immediately respond to an email requesting comment. It wasn't clear whether Hazan had an attorney. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York didn't immediately respond to a voicemail left by The Associated Press.
The three were arrested between June and September — Soall and Hazan in Spain and Sheetrit in the U.K. Extradition requests for all three are pending.
In 2008, Hazan was convicted in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.
The trio, who have nicknames that include "Rocky Balboa," "Superman Cash" and "Fat Boy," often targeted the companies' accounting departments. They would send an email purporting to be from the CEO and ask for help with a confidential financial transaction, according to court documents.
They would also coordinate a phone or video call where the defendants used AI to mimic the voice and sometimes the image of the CEO, according to the indictment.
